lessons.title: Creating and mounting ext4, xfs and btrfs
lessons.goal:
Learn the steps from a raw block device to a usable directory: `mkfs`, `mount`, use, `umount`, and compare the three main Linux file systems.

Why it matters: choosing and creating a file system is a day-one admin task. Each has different strengths, and you cannot shrink some of them later.

setup.note: These steps use sudo, loop devices and RAM-light image files. They never touch real disks. Each lesson unmounts and detaches everything at the end.

steps.title: A file system turns blocks into files
steps.text: A raw disk is just numbered blocks. A **file system** adds structure: directories, names, permissions, free space tracking. `mkfs.TYPE` writes that structure (the **superblock**, inode tables, free-space maps). Our current root file system:

steps.title: ext4
steps.text: The traditional Linux file system: robust, journaled, can grow and shrink (offline). We create a 256 MB image, attach it, format it and mount it.

run.cmd: sudo mkfs.ext4 -q $L1; sudo mkdir -p /tmp/lab/m1 && sudo mount $L1 /tmp/lab/m1 && sudo chown $(id -un): /tmp/lab/m1

steps.after: `lost+found` is created by ext4 for `fsck` to put recovered fragments in.

steps.title: xfs
steps.text: A high-performance journaled file system, strong with big files and parallel I/O, default on Red Hat family systems. It can **grow but not shrink**.

run.cmd: sudo mkfs.xfs -q $L2; sudo mkdir -p /tmp/lab/m2 && sudo mount $L2 /tmp/lab/m2 && sudo chown $(id -un): /tmp/lab/m2

run.output:
meta-data=DEV             isize=512    agcount=4, agsize=32768 blks
data     =                       bsize=4096   blocks=131072, imaxpct=25

steps.title: btrfs
steps.text: A copy-on-write file system with checksums, snapshots, subvolumes and compression built in. It can grow and shrink online.

run.cmd: sudo mkfs.btrfs -q $L3; sudo mkdir -p /tmp/lab/m3 && sudo mount $L3 /tmp/lab/m3 && sudo chown $(id -un): /tmp/lab/m3

steps.title: Compare and clean up
steps.text: All three are now mounted in the same tree, and programs cannot tell them apart. Unmount before you detach the device.

run.cmd: sudo umount /tmp/lab/m1 /tmp/lab/m2 /tmp/lab/m3; sudo losetup -d $L1 $L2 $L3; echo detached

steps.under: Choosing: **ext4** when you want the most proven general-purpose choice; **xfs** for large file systems and heavy parallel workloads (and you will not need to shrink); **btrfs** (or ZFS) when you want snapshots, checksums and cheap clones. The VFS (module 17) hides the differences from programs.

options: Writes the file system structures to a device
quiz.explain: It creates the superblock, inode tables and so on.

quiz.q: Which of these file systems cannot be shrunk?
Which is created by ext4 for fsck to place recovered files?
Which file system has built-in snapshots?

check.scenario: A new 20 TB data volume will hold huge video files with many parallel readers and writers. Which file system do you pick, and what must you accept?
check.answer: **xfs**: it scales to large file systems and parallel I/O. Accept that it cannot be shrunk (plan the size) and that repairs use `xfs_repair` offline. Format with `mkfs.xfs` and mount with `noatime` if access times are not needed.

lessons.title: /etc/fstab and mount options
lessons.goal:
Learn the six fields of `/etc/fstab`, how to test a line **before** a reboot, and how mount options such as `ro`, `noexec` and `nosuid` change behaviour.

Why it matters: a wrong fstab line can stop a server from booting. Options are a cheap and effective security and safety tool.

setup.note: These steps use sudo, loop devices and RAM-light image files. They never touch real disks. Each lesson unmounts and detaches everything at the end.

steps.title: A file system to practise on
steps.text: We create an ext4 image and read its UUID.

run.cmd: truncate -s 64M fs.img; L=$(sudo losetup -f --show fs.img); sudo mkfs.ext4 -q $L; U=$(sudo blkid -s UUID -o value $L); echo "UUID has ${#U} characters"

steps.title: The six fields
steps.text:
A line in `/etc/fstab` has six fields:

1. **device** (best: `UUID=...`)
2. **mount point**
3. **file system type**
4. **options** (comma separated)
5. **dump** flag (0 = ignore; legacy)
6. **fsck order** (1 for root, 2 for others, 0 = skip)

We write a sample file of our own, not the real fstab.

run.cmd: echo "UUID=$U /tmp/lab/mnt ext4 defaults,noexec,nosuid 0 2" > sample.fstab; sed "s/$U/<uuid>/" sample.fstab

steps.title: Verify before you reboot
steps.text: `findmnt --verify` checks a table for mistakes (missing mount point, unknown type, missing device). Run it on the real `/etc/fstab` after every edit. `mount -a` also tests all lines at once.

run.output: Success, no errors or warnings detected

steps.title: Mount using the table
steps.text: `mount -T FILE MOUNTPOINT` reads the entry for that mount point from the given table.

run.cmd: sudo mount -T sample.fstab /tmp/lab/mnt && findmnt -no OPTIONS /tmp/lab/mnt | tr ',' '\n' | grep -E '^(rw|noexec|nosuid)$' | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.title: noexec blocks running programs
steps.text: With `noexec`, files on the file system cannot be executed. Attackers who can write to a directory like `/tmp` often try to run a program from there, so many systems mount it `noexec`.

steps.title: ro, and remount
steps.text: `remount` changes options on a live mount. A read-only file system rejects all writes with `Read-only file system`. The kernel also remounts a damaged file system read-only on its own, to protect the data (lab: read-only filesystem).

run.output: touch: cannot touch '/tmp/lab/mnt/x': Read-only file system

run.cmd: sudo mount -o remount,rw /tmp/lab/mnt; sudo touch /tmp/lab/mnt/x && echo 'write works again'
sudo umount /tmp/lab/mnt; sudo losetup -d $L; echo cleaned

steps.under: `mount` calls the `mount(2)` system call with the device, target, type, flags and a string of file-system-specific options. Flags like `MS_NOEXEC` are stored in the **mount** (not in the file system), which is why the same disk can be mounted `rw` here and `ro` elsewhere, and why bind mounts can have different options.

quiz.q: What is the sixth field of an fstab line?
quiz.explain: 0 skips fsck; 1 is for the root file system; 2 for the rest.

quiz.q: Which command checks an fstab file for errors?

options: Forbids executing programs from the file system

quiz.q: What does the option `nofail` do in fstab?
options: Boot continues if the device is missing
quiz.explain: A missing non-essential disk does not stop boot.

check.scenario: You added a line for a new data disk to /etc/fstab, ran `reboot`, and the server never came back (emergency mode). How do you avoid and fix this?
check.answer: Avoid: use UUIDs, add `nofail` for non-critical disks, and run `findmnt --verify` and `mount -a` before rebooting. Fix: log in on the console, `mount -o remount,rw /`, correct or comment the line in `/etc/fstab`, `systemctl daemon-reload`, and reboot.

lessons.title: Journaling, fsck repair and copy-on-write
lessons.goal:
Learn how a journal makes a file system crash-safe, repair a deliberately damaged ext4 with `e2fsck`, and see how btrfs copy-on-write makes clones free.

Why it matters: after a crash or a power loss you must know what the file system promises, how to check it, and when a repair is safe.

setup.note: These steps use sudo, loop devices and RAM-light image files. They never touch real disks. Each lesson unmounts and detaches everything at the end.

steps.title: The journal
steps.text: A crash in the middle of a metadata update (for example: allocate a block, update the inode, update the directory) could leave the file system inconsistent. A **journal** is a log area: the file system first writes what it is about to do, then does it. After a crash it replays or discards the log, in seconds, instead of scanning the whole disk.

run.cmd: truncate -s 128M ext4.img; L=$(sudo losetup -f --show ext4.img); sudo mkfs.ext4 -q $L
sudo dumpe2fs -h $L 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^(Filesystem features|Journal size|Journal features)' | cut -c1-100
run.output:
Filesystem features:      has_journal ext_attr resize_inode dir_index filetype extent 64bit flex_bg 
Journal features:         (none)

steps.title: fsck on a clean file system
steps.text: `e2fsck -fn` forces a full check (`-f`) and only reports (`-n`): it changes nothing. Exit code 0 means no problems.

run.output:
e2fsck 1.47.1 (20-May-2024)
Pass 1: Checking inodes, blocks, and sizes
Pass 2: Checking directory structure
Pass 3: Checking directory connectivity
Pass 4: Checking reference counts
Pass 5: Checking group summary information
/dev/loop0: 11/32768 files (0.0% non-contiguous), 13883/131072 blocks
exit code: 0

steps.title: Damage it on purpose
steps.text: We create a file, unmount, and then **clear its inode** with `debugfs`. The directory still lists the name, but the inode is gone: a typical corruption.

run.cmd: sudo mkdir -p /tmp/lab/m1 && sudo mount $L /tmp/lab/m1 && sudo sh -c 'echo precious > /tmp/lab/m1/victim.txt'; ino=$(stat -c %i /tmp/lab/m1/victim.txt); echo "inode of victim.txt: $ino"
sudo umount /tmp/lab/m1; sudo debugfs -w -R "clri <$ino>" $L 2>&1 | tail -n 1; echo cleared

steps.title: Check, then repair
steps.text: Always run a read-only check first. Then repair with `-y` (answer yes). `fsck` must run on an **unmounted** file system.

run.output:
Pass 1: Checking inodes, blocks, and sizes
Pass 2: Checking directory structure
Entry 'victim.txt' in / (2) has deleted/unused inode 12.  Clear? no

Entry 'victim.txt' in / (2) has an incorrect filetype (was 1, should be 0).
exit code: 4

Pass 1: Checking inodes, blocks, and sizes
Pass 2: Checking directory structure
Entry 'victim.txt' in / (2) has deleted/unused inode 12.  Clear? yes

steps.under: `fsck` works pass by pass: inodes, directory structure, connectivity (every inode reachable), reference counts, and the free-space bitmaps. A journal only protects against **crash** inconsistency, not against bad blocks, bugs or someone running `clri`. Always keep backups: repair can lose data.
steps.after: The first check lists the problems and exits with 4 (errors left uncorrected). `-fy` clears the dangling directory entry (the file is lost) and fixes the counters. The last check is clean.

steps.title: Copy-on-write on btrfs
steps.text: btrfs never overwrites live data: it writes new blocks and then switches the pointers. This makes a **reflink** copy free: two files share the same blocks until one changes.

run.cmd: sudo losetup -d $L; truncate -s 256M btrfs.img; B=$(sudo losetup -f --show btrfs.img); sudo mkfs.btrfs -q $B; sudo mkdir -p /tmp/lab/m3; sudo mount $B /tmp/lab/m3; sudo chown $(id -un): /tmp/lab/m3
dd if=/dev/urandom of=/tmp/lab/m3/big bs=1M count=20 status=none; cp --reflink=always /tmp/lab/m3/big /tmp/lab/m3/clone; sync
sudo btrfs filesystem du -s /tmp/lab/m3 | awk 'NR==1 {print} NR==2 {print $1, $2, $3}'
sudo umount /tmp/lab/m3; sudo losetup -d $B; echo cleaned

steps.after: Two 20 MB files, but the data is stored **once**: Total is 40 MB, Exclusive is 0 (nothing belongs to one file only) and the whole 20 MB is Set shared.

quiz.q: What does a journal protect against?
quiz.explain: It lets the file system recover quickly after an unclean shutdown.

quiz.q: When must you run fsck on a file system?
quiz.explain: Repairing a mounted file system corrupts it.

quiz.q: What is a reflink copy on btrfs?
options: A copy that shares data blocks with the original until changed

check.scenario: After a power loss an xfs file system refuses to mount: `mount: wrong fs type, bad superblock`, log corruption. What are the steps?
check.answer: Unmount if mounted, then try `mount` once more (it replays the log). If the log is bad: `xfs_repair -n DEV` (dry run), then `xfs_repair DEV`; only if it says the log is dirty and cannot be replayed use `xfs_repair -L` (zeroes the log: **last resort**, recent changes are lost). Restore from backup if the data matters.

interview.q: What is a journal in a file system?
interview.a: A log where the file system records pending metadata changes before applying them, so after a crash it can replay or discard them quickly. See [the lesson](#/lesson/20/journal-fsck-cow).
ext4: proven, general, can shrink offline. xfs: scalable, parallel I/O, cannot shrink. btrfs: copy-on-write, snapshots, checksums, compression. See [the lesson](#/lesson/20/mkfs-and-mount).
device (UUID), mount point, type, options, dump, fsck order. See [the lesson](#/lesson/20/fstab-and-mount-options).

interview.q: How do you avoid an unbootable server after editing fstab?
interview.a: Use UUIDs, `nofail` for non-critical disks, and test with `findmnt --verify` and `mount -a` before rebooting.

interview.q: How do you repair a damaged ext4 file system?
interview.a: Unmount it, run `e2fsck -fn` to see the damage, then `e2fsck -fy` to repair; restore from backup for lost data. Use `xfs_repair` for xfs.
noexec: no program execution from the mount. nosuid: ignore setuid/setgid bits. nodev: ignore device files. Used on /tmp, /var/tmp and removable media.

glossary.def: The on-disk structure that organises files, directories and free space on a block device.
The file system's main metadata block: size, features, UUID.
/etc/fstab: the table of file systems to mount at boot.
A setting such as ro, noexec or nosuid applied to a mount.
A log of pending metadata changes used for fast crash recovery.
File system consistency check and repair tool.
Writing changed data to new blocks instead of overwriting; enables cheap snapshots and clones.
